rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following a means is traveling by a path or route between east and west, using landmarks and stopping points.
rows.anchor: a path or a route (IK, Ṭ, Ṭs) between east and west (Ṭ), following landmarks and various stopping points (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Because God gave Dhu’l-Qarnayn the means to all things, he used the means available to attain whatever he desired.
rows.anchor: al-Rāzī says that when he desired something, he would follow these means to attain it (R)

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: The setting sun in a murky spring describes how sunset appeared to the human eye rather than a literal setting in a spring.
rows.anchor: not understood literally by most commentators, but is rather thought to describe how the setting sun would appear to the human eye

rows.speaker: IK, R
rows.claim: If Dhu’l-Qarnayn is Alexander, the westernmost known land bordered the ocean, where the distant sunset appeared to enter dark water.
rows.anchor: the westernmost point of the land known to Dhu’l-Qarnayn (if understood as referring to Alexander) was bordered by the ocean (IK, R)

rows.speaker: IK, R
rows.claim: Legend placed the people Dhu’l-Qarnayn found in a city with twelve thousand gates.
rows.anchor: according to legend, residing in a city of twelve thousand gates (IK, R)

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs
rows.claim: The context suggests the people were disbelievers or idolaters.
rows.anchor: The context of the verse suggests that Dhu’l-Qarnayn found this people

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: One interpretation of the choice to punish them is to slay them for continuing in idolatry.
rows.anchor: punish them, that is, slay them for their persistence in idolatry (R, Ṭs, Z)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Treating them kindly can mean calling them to Islam, worship of the One God, and guidance.
rows.anchor: call them to islām—that is, to submission to and worship of the One God—and should seek to guide them (Z)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Alternatively, treating them well can mean being generous and forgiving toward them.
rows.anchor: or that he should be generous and forgiving toward them (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhu’l-Qarnayn chose to call them to Islam; rejecters would be punished and believers rewarded.
rows.anchor: Dhu’l-Qarnayn chose to call them to islām, indicating that those who rejected his call would be punished (v. 87), while those who believed would receive a most beautiful reward (v. 88)

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs
rows.claim: Direct divine instruction suggests Dhu’l-Qarnayn received revelation, supporting the view that he was a prophet.
rows.anchor: a prophet (R, Ṭs), although others understand God’s instructions

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others understand God’s instructions as inspiration rather than revelation.
rows.anchor: although others understand God’s instructions to him as

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: The wrongdoers here are those who associated partners with God.
rows.anchor: refers to those who ascribed partners unto God (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: R, IK
rows.claim: They persisted in disbelief after Dhu’l-Qarnayn called them to monotheism.
rows.anchor: persisted in disbelief (R) after having been called to monotheistic belief by Dhu’l-Qarnayn (IK)

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs
rows.claim: The punishment in this life is their being slain for disbelief; the later terrible punishment is in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: their being slain in this life as punishment for their disbelief (R, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The believers and righteous workers are those who respond to Dhu’l-Qarnayn’s call to monotheistic worship.
rows.anchor: refers to those who do so after Dhu’l-Qarnayn calls the people to monotheistic worship (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both faith and good deeds are requirements for entering the Garden, as many verses reiterate.
rows.anchor: Both faith and good deeds are requirements for entry into the paradisal Garden, as is repeated in dozens of verses

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: One reading takes the most beautiful reward to mean that the reward itself is most beautiful.
rows.anchor: the reward itself is that which is most beautiful (R)

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: An alternative reads it as a reward for the most beautiful deed: the testimony of divine Oneness or faith and righteous work.
rows.anchor: it may mean “have a reward [for the deed] which is most beautiful” (R, Z)

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: The easy command may mean imposing mandatory alms and land tax only in an easy degree and manner.
rows.anchor: easy for them to fulfill (R, Z)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Alternatively, the easy command simply means Dhu’l-Qarnayn would treat them kindly.
rows.anchor: or it may simply mean that he will treat them with kindness (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following a means here means taking a path, as in 18:85–86.
rows.anchor: For followed a means, that is, a path, see 18:85–86c

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rising place is the easternmost point of human civilization, and the shelterless people lacked protection from the sun.
rows.anchor: the easternmost point of human civilization, he found a people for whom We had not made any shelter from it, that is, from the sun

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Commentators describe a land without mountains or trees for shade and without buildings or other shelters.
rows.anchor: neither mountains nor trees for natural shade, nor buildings or other structures for shelter from the sun (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: JJ, Z
rows.claim: Some suggest the land could not support buildings.
rows.anchor: the land could not sustain buildings (JJ, Z)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Another suggestion is that the people did not know how to build structures.
rows.anchor: these people had no knowledge of how to build structures (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: They escaped the sun by going into water or underground tunnels, then emerged after midday as the sun began to set.
rows.anchor: they would emerge again(Ṭ, Z)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Some say Dhu’l-Qarnayn received the same divine mandate for these people as for those at sunset.
rows.anchor: Dhu’l-Qarnayn was given the same Divine mandate regarding this people as he was given for those in the region of the setting sun (v. 86; Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: God’s encompassing knowledge can refer to His knowledge of the strange people Dhu’l-Qarnayn encountered.
rows.anchor: He had knowledge of these strange people whom Dhu’l-Qarnayn encountered (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Alternatively, “that which was with him” means God knew Dhu’l-Qarnayn’s armies, tools, and other means.
rows.anchor: armies, tools, and other means that Dhu’l-Qarnayn possessed (IK, Ṭs, Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following a means again means taking a path, as in 18:85–86.
rows.anchor: For followed a means, that is, a path, see 18:85–86c

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Most commentators identify the two barriers as the Armenia and Azerbaijan mountains, a barrier to lands farther north.
rows.anchor: most widely reported by commentators to refer to the mountains of Armenia and Azerbaijan, which formed a “barrier” to lands and peoples lying farther north (R, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The place between the barriers is an opening between the mountains, with the people on their near or southern side.
rows.anchor: in an opening between the mountains (Ṭ), he found a people dwelling on the near (or southern) side of the mountains

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: One explanation is that they spoke a language understood only by themselves, not other languages.
rows.anchor: they spoke a language they alone could understand and they could understand no other (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Alternatively, they could understand others only with great difficulty or through gestures.
rows.anchor: they could only understand others with great difficulty or by means of gestures (R)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Dhu’l-Qarnayn may have understood them through a special God-given ability, like Solomon’s knowledge of bird speech.
rows.anchor: God gave him a special ability to understand their language, as He had given Solomon knowledge of the language of the birds (27:16; Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Another explanation is that a translator enabled communication.
rows.anchor: or because there was a translator (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Gog and Magog are also called Yājūj or Ājūj and Mājūj in Arabic literature.
rows.anchor: also called Yājūj (or Ājūj) and Mājūj elsewhere in Arabic literature (R, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Commentators report Gog and Magog as descendants of Noah’s son Japheth.
rows.anchor: the offspring of Noah’s son Japheth (IK, Ṭs, Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Genesis 10:2 lists Magog among Japheth’s sons.
rows.anchor: Genesis 10:2, where Magog is listed as one of Japheth’s sons

rows.speaker: IK, R, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Some speculate that Gog and Magog were ancestors or distant relatives of the Turks.
rows.anchor: ancestors or distant relatives of the Turks (IK, R, Ṭs, Z)

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: Another speculation identifies them as possibly related to the Daylamites of northern Iran.
rows.anchor: possibly the Daylamites (who hailed from regions to the north of Iran; R, Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ethnic speculations appear based on the peoples’ fearsome reputation as warriors for medieval Muslims.
rows.anchor: such speculations seem to be based upon the rather fearsome reputation these two peoples had as warriors for medieval Muslims

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Some derive Yaʾjūj or Ājūj from a word for igniting fire, and Maʾjūj from a word for sea waves, both destructive forces.
rows.anchor: Yaʾjūj or Ājūj may derive from taʾajjuj, meaning to ignite a fire, and Maʾjūj from mawj, referring to the waves of the sea (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hebrew scripture depicts Gog of Magog attacking Israel, while Revelation calls Gog and Magog nations Satan will rouse in the end times.
rows.anchor: in Ezekiel 38:2, the prophet Ezekiel is told to prophesy against Gog, of the land of Magog, who would attack Israel; and in Revelation 20:8, Gog and Magog refer to the nations that Satan will rouse to fight with him in the end times

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: A hadith describes Gog and Magog as huge.
rows.anchor: A ḥadīth describes Gog and Magog as huge in size (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Other speculative reports portray them as very small or very large, with wild-beast claws and teeth.
rows.anchor: speculative reports describe them variously as very small in stature or very large (R), with the claws and teeth of wild beasts (R)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: A report says each male begets a thousand armed offspring, who eat every kind of beast.
rows.anchor: each male among them was said to beget a thousand offspring, all of whom bear arms and eat from every manner of beast on the earth (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Workers of corruption” denotes both spiritual corruption and violent, wicked behavior, elsewhere in the Quran.
rows.anchor: a term used throughout the Quran to indicate spiritual corruption as well as violent and wicked behavior on the earth

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Their corruption is said to include devouring people and the land’s food and resources, inflicting torment and slaughter.
rows.anchor: they used to devour people (R, Ṭ) as well as all the food and resources of the land (R, Ṭs, Z), and that the people had suffered much torment and slaughter from them (Ṭs, Z)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: The people offered tribute as payment for Dhu’l-Qarnayn to build the barrier.
rows.anchor: some form of payment for setting up the barrier between themselves and Gog and Magog (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: Another interpretation places Gog and Magog’s corruption later, near the Hour, in the eschatological events described in hadith and Islamic sources.
rows.anchor: this verse refers to Gog and Magog working corruption on earth at a later point, near the time of the approach of the Hour (Ṭ, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Symbolically, Gog and Magog may represent destructive tendencies in psyche and religious culture near the end times, as traditional barriers weaken.
rows.anchor: Gog and Magog may be identified with the various negative and destructive developments in the human psyche and religious culture

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran also describes their future destruction at the end times, when they rush from every hill as the promise draws near.
rows.anchor: 21:96–97, which refers to the future destruction Gog and Magog will wreak at this time

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs
rows.claim: Dhu’l-Qarnayn’s God-given wealth and extensive lands meant he had no need of their payment.
rows.anchor: God had given him such great wealth and expanse of land that he had no need of what they could offer him (R, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: He undertook the work simply to pursue righteousness and do good.
rows.anchor: he would provide this service simply for the sake of righteousness and doing good (IK)

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī, Ibn Kathīr
rows.claim: They compare his response to Solomon declining the Queen of Sheba’s gifts in 27:36.
rows.anchor: the response is similar to that of Solomon in 27:36 when given gifts by the Queen of Sheba

rows.speaker: IK, R, Ṭs
rows.claim: Dhu’l-Qarnayn asked for able-bodied men, tools, and materials to help build the barrier.
rows.anchor: provide him with able-bodied men and the tools and materials to assist him in making the barrier (IK, R, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: JJ, Ṭs
rows.claim: He filled the gap between the cliffs with iron pieces or ingots to level them.
rows.anchor: filling in the gap between them with the pieces, or ingots, of iron (JJ, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: JJ, Ṭs
rows.claim: He ordered the people to blow fire on the iron until the mass became intensely hot or flaming.
rows.anchor: blow fire on iron pieces now filling the mountain opening until the heap of iron was itself intensely hot or flaming (JJ, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: JJ, Ṭs
rows.claim: The poured metal is interpreted as molten copper, brass, or iron, filling gaps and making a solid wall.
rows.anchor: molten copper, or alternately molten brass or iron, over the burning iron barrier to fill in the holes between the iron pieces (JJ, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: The finished barrier could not be climbed over or breached through.
rows.anchor: which Gog and Magog were unable to surmount from above or breach from below (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Although most commentators place the mountains in Armenia and Azerbaijan, some locate them near the meeting of the Mediterranean and Atlantic.
rows.anchor: some say the two mountains were located near where the Roman (Mediterranean) sea meets the (Atlantic) ocean (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The mercy may be the constructed barrier itself or Dhu’l-Qarnayn’s ability to build it, protecting people from Gog and Magog.
rows.anchor: this barrier he had constructed, or else the ability to construct it (R), was a mercy from his Lord to hold back the terrors of Gog and Magog

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Some place the Promise at the onset of the Hour’s events, after Jesus kills the Antichrist.
rows.anchor: with the onset of the events of the Hour, only after Jesus has killed the Antichrist, according to some (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Another description places the Promise as Resurrection draws near.
rows.anchor: as the time of Resurrection draws near (R)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: When the Promise arrives, God will crumble the barrier to dust and level it.
rows.anchor: God would crumble the barrier to dust and level it to the ground(Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The barrier’s destruction parallels Quranic descriptions of mountains being destroyed at the Hour.
rows.anchor: descriptions of God’s destruction of the mountains in general with the coming of the Hour

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Some connect the account with Khiḍr, who with Elisha is said to meet nightly at the barrier to keep Gog and Magog in.
rows.anchor: Khiḍr and Elisha (al-Yasaʿ; see 6:86; 38:48) meet every night at this mountain barrier to prevent Gog and Magog from getting out (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The truth of God’s Promise is reiterated in several other verses.
rows.anchor: The Promise of God is true is repeated in several verses

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: “That Day” is the Last Day before Resurrection but after the Antichrist is slain.
rows.anchor: the Last Day, before the Resurrection but after the slaying of the Antichrist (IK)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: One view identifies the surging forces as Gog and Magog and humans whose lives and property they overtake.
rows.anchor: Gog and Magog and human beings, whose lives and property they are overtaking (IK)

rows.speaker: Aj, IK
rows.claim: Another view identifies them as humans and jinn coming against one another.
rows.anchor: human beings and jinn, who come against one another at this time (Aj, IK)

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Some say the surging forces will be unable to enter Makkah, Madinah, or Jerusalem.
rows.anchor: will not, however, be able to enter Makkah, Madinah, or Jerusalem (Aj)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The trumpet heralds the onset of Resurrection.
rows.anchor: the trumpet shall be blown, heralding the onset of the Day of Resurrection

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The trumpet is said to be blown by Seraphiel (Isrāfīl) or another archangel.
rows.anchor: blown by Seraphiel (Isrāfīl) or one of the other archangels (IK)

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: God presents Hell so disbelievers see it and hear its raging and groaning before entering.
rows.anchor: so that they can see it and hear its raging and groaning (Aj), even before they enter it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The veiled and deaf are spiritually blind and deaf in life, impervious to prophetic revelation and God’s Oneness.
rows.anchor: spiritually blind and deaf in life, making them impervious to the revealed messages of the prophets and to the Oneness of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People have no helpers apart from God, and the Quran repeatedly warns against seeking other protectors.
rows.anchor: people have no helpers apart from God (see, e.g., 42:46) and repeatedly warns those who would vainly seek protectors other than Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Such false protectors include idols, Satan, and his minions; the Quran likens them to the spider’s fragile house.
rows.anchor: such as idols (2:257) or Satan and his minions (7:30; 18:50). See 29:41

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling Hell a welcome is ironic, like promising disbelievers glad tidings of punishment or calling Hell a refuge.
rows.anchor: may be considered a somewhat ironic usage, similar to those verses in which the disbelievers are given glad tidings of a painful punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell’s punishment is also called a welcome elsewhere, in contrast to the Garden’s welcome for believers.
rows.anchor: Hell and its punishments are also described as a welcome in 56:52–56; 56:92–94. Cf. v. 107

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell recompenses those who mock God’s signs and messengers by denying them and belittling their warnings.
rows.anchor: mock God’s signs and messengers by denying them and belittling their warnings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Garden welcomes believers who perform righteous deeds, just as Hell is a welcome for disbelievers.
rows.anchor: Just as Hell is a “welcome” for the disbelievers, the Garden is a welcome for those who believe and perform righteous deeds

rows.speaker: ST, Z
rows.claim: “The Words of my Lord” may mean God’s Knowledge and Wisdom.
rows.anchor: a reference to God’s Knowledge and Wisdom (ST, Z)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Alternatively, the phrase can mean the many spiritual meanings and benefits of the Quran and other revelation, not merely its literal words.
rows.anchor: the many spiritual meanings and benefits of the Quran and other Divine Revelation (Ṭs), rather than to the literal words of the Quran itself

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: The phrase may also mean God’s capacity to create and command whatever He wills through the Word.
rows.anchor: His capacity to create and to command whatever He wills (Ṭs), for God creates by the “Word,” as in 2:117

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: In this context, some take the Words as promises of afterlife rewards and punishments.
rows.anchor: the rewards promised and punishments threatened in the Hereafter (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Another contextual reading is the generous words God will speak to the people of the Garden in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: the generous words God will speak to the people of the Garden in the Hereafter (Aj)

rows.speaker: Aj, R, ST
rows.claim: All these meanings exceed the finite sea because God’s Words are infinite and eternal.
rows.anchor: as vast as the sea is, it is still finite, while the Words of God are infinite (Aj, R) and eternal (ST)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same image appears in 31:27, where even the trees as pens and the sea with seven more seas would not exhaust God’s Words.
rows.anchor: See also commentary on 31:27: And if all the trees on earth were pens

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad and other prophets state they are human beings delivering a message from God.
rows.anchor: the Prophet Muhammad and other prophets assert that they are only a human being delivering a message from God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prophets’ human nature itself causes some people to doubt their message.
rows.anchor: it is the merely human nature of prophets itself that causes some people to doubt them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hoping to meet God entails belief, righteous deeds, and avoiding shirk, the unforgivable sin of idolatry.
rows.anchor: should perform righteous deeds and should ascribe no partners to God; that is, they must avoid the unforgivable sin of shirk, or idolatry

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAjībah
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAjībah cites a hadith warning believers against minor shirk, which the Prophet explains as hypocrisy or religious ostentation.
rows.anchor: Ibn ʿAjībah cites in connection with this verse

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: Asked to define minor shirk, the Prophet said it meant hypocrisy or religious ostentation.
rows.anchor: the Prophet responded that it referred to hypocrisy or religious ostentation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These opening separated letters occur at the start of twenty-nine surahs.
rows.anchor: found at the beginning of twenty-nine sūrahs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maryam is the only surah beginning with this letter sequence, the longest set of separated letters in one verse.
rows.anchor: the only one that begins with these particular letters, which constitute the longest set of such letters found in a single verse

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators hold that the letters’ meaning is not clearly known.
rows.anchor: the meaning of these letters is considered by most commentators to not be known clearly

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some speculate that the letters may stand for divine Names and Attributes, such as Kabīr or Karīm for Kāf.
rows.anchor: letters at the beginning of this sūrah may stand for various Names and Attributes of God found in the Quran

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Others take the individually pronounced sequence as a name of God or a name for the Quran.
rows.anchor: constitute one of the Names of God or else a name for the Quran (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fuller discussion of separated letters is found at 2:1.
rows.anchor: For a fuller commentary on the separated letters, see 2:1c
